content.intro: This lesson covers Entering Data into Excel as part of Data Entry and Cell Management. It follows the attached Excel curriculum, with an emphasis on small examples and verification.
content.why_it_matters: Entering Data into Excel establishes the workbook structure and data-quality habits that later formulas and reports depend on. A clear layout reduces avoidable editing mistakes and makes the workbook easier for another person to understand.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Entering Data into Excel focuses on the following parts of the supplied syllabus: Text, numbers, dates, and times; Entering data into individual cells; Confirming and cancelling cell entries; Data-entry conventions. Keep the underlying source data visible and make each assumption explicit.

content_blocks.expected_output: Calculates a date/time result using serial values; the exact interpretation depends on cell values, formatting, locale and whether holidays or overnight intervals matter.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Enter real Excel date/time values, not ambiguous text. Apply an appropriate number format and test boundaries such as month-end, blanks and overnight durations.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Work in a duplicate workbook or a scratch sheet. Restore the input range and formula/code to the original state, clear filters or selections, then rerun the same test cases. Record expected and actual behavior rather than assuming a successful result.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Start with a small, known dataset for entering data into excel. Apply the example above, compute or inspect at least one result independently, then deliberately try a blank, duplicate, boundary, or not-found case where relevant.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small worksheet or workbook section that demonstrates entering data into excel. Use clear headers, label units and assumptions, and capture expected versus actual output for a normal case and an edge case. Where the concept requires a specialized Excel feature, first verify that feature is available in your Excel edition.

content.task: Build or inspect an Excel example that demonstrates entering data into excel; use the example to verify one normal and one edge case, and write down any version or tool dependency. For a complete curriculum practice scenario, also complete “Personal Information Sheet” using the synthetic dataset `assets/data/practical-01-personal-information-sheet.csv`; see the linked additional exercise file.
task_acceptance_criteria: The worksheet/workflow uses a clear, labeled source range and explicit assumptions.
The learner records an expected output and independently compares it with the actual result.
At least one relevant edge case is checked; data and formula errors are not silently concealed.
The workbook is saved as a copy and compatibility/security/accessibility notes are followed where relevant.
hints: Reduce the problem to a small range with known values before scaling it up.
Inspect cell values and formulas, not only displayed formatting; verify data types, references and range boundaries.
Compare expected versus actual results and check the Microsoft documentation for version-specific functions or tools.
content.expected_output: Calculates a date/time result using serial values; the exact interpretation depends on cell values, formatting, locale and whether holidays or overnight intervals matter.
common_mistakes: Assuming the displayed format is the same as the stored value or data type.
Using an incorrect range boundary, a mismatched lookup key, or an unverified assumption.
Trusting a result without comparing it with a known calculation or checking a failure/edge case.
summary: Entering Data into Excel supports the workflow in Data Entry and Cell Management.
Use a small example, make assumptions visible, and verify the result against the source.
Check target-version availability and keep a clean copy before making high-impact changes.
